messages.text:
**My argument attacks the predictive force of Fátima—not whether people sincerely experienced something extraordinary.**

Your core argument, as I understand it, is: **a public miracle was announced months beforehand, and an extraordinary event then occurred before a huge crowd on the appointed day. That strongly favors Marian intervention.**

My counterargument is that **the announcement could help produce its own apparent fulfillment**:

1. **It gathered the audience and established what they were waiting for.** The recorded promise specified a public sign and date, but did not specify the subsequent solar movements, colors or descent. [Early interrogation records](https://www.fatima.pt/files/upload/fontes/F001_DCF_selecao.pdf)
2. **The witnesses shared viewing conditions and communicated.** Avelino de Almeida’s contemporary account describes the crowd turning toward the solar disc and people asking one another what they saw. Those are documented conditions for shared attention and interpretation. They do not prove suggestion caused everything. [Almeida’s October 15 report](https://fatima-1917.com/pt/d/iii-1-87)
3. **Ordinary visual mechanisms can produce genuine unusual experiences.** Qasim Zaidi and colleagues at **SUNY College of Optometry** experimentally demonstrated color afterimages at ordinary light levels. That supports a component of the proposed explanation, although it does **not** reproduce Fátima’s reported descending disc or the complete event. [Primary study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3562597/)

The resulting argument is: **the prediction, crowd and reports need not be three unrelated coincidences under an ordinary explanation; the prediction helped organize the circumstances of observation.** Consequently, their combination may discriminate between ordinary and supernatural causes less strongly than you argue.

**Its present weakness:** I still have to account for the strongest environmental and distant-witness reports, and establish that the proposed mechanisms adequately fit the reported experience. Until then, this is a substantive competing argument—not a demonstrated defeat of your Fátima case.

The tally is **2–0**; this challenge is open.

messages.text:
**His strongest testimony is that he personally saw an extraordinary moving, color-changing solar disc—not merely an excited crowd.**

1. **A disc people could look at comfortably.** In *O Século* on October 15, he describes a matte-silver appearance that could be viewed without effort, glare or discomfort. This establishes his reported viewing experience, rather than a medical examination for retinal injury. [Original account](https://fatima-1917.com/pt/d/iii-1-87)

2. **Violent apparent movement.** In his October 29 follow-up, he explicitly places the solar spectacle among things he himself saw, describing a **“violent and convulsive dance.”** That makes his personal testimony clearer than passages in the first article describing the crowd’s reports. [October 29 account](https://fatima-1917.com/pt/d/iii-1-228)

3. **Successive brilliant colors.** That same firsthand description says the solar surface took on beautiful, brilliant colors in succession. [October 29 account](https://fatima-1917.com/pt/d/iii-1-228)

4. **Rain stopped and clouds broke at the announced hour.** He connects the timing of the weather change and solar appearance with the expected sign. [October 29 account](https://fatima-1917.com/pt/d/iii-1-228)

5. **Immediate private confirmation.** In a postcard to his sister dated October 13, he wrote, **“I saw extraordinary things,”** and estimated roughly 40,000 present. This supports an immediate personal impression, independently of his later public elaboration. [Postcard](https://fatima-1917.com/pt/d/iii-1-54)

**The descending-disc claim needs careful attribution:** his October 15 article records people saying it descended almost enough to burn the earth. That passage attributes descent to other witnesses; it is less secure as Almeida’s own personal observation. [October 15 report](https://fatima-1917.com/pt/d/iii-1-87)

He expressly left the cause undecided. **For my proposed ordinary explanation, his personally reported violent motion and comfortable viewing are substantial observations that need answering—not details I can dismiss as somebody else’s story.**

Yes. **“They expected something” falls well short of explaining what they reported seeing.** Almeida himself described a comfortably viewable silver disc, apparent violent movement and successive brilliant colors—not merely a crowd becoming excited. His testimony gives that objection particular force. [Almeida’s October 29 account](https://fatima-1917.com/pt/d/iii-1-228)

A shared ordinary visual stimulus could affect a very large crowd, including skeptics, so crowd size alone doesn’t exclude that possibility. Your response therefore substantially limits my “priming the pump” objection: the announcement explains why people gathered and watched; it does not, by itself, explain what followed. I have not earned a point against your core argument here.

Here’s our map, with the [interactive version available here](research/fatima-distant-witnesses-20261027/map-preview.html).

[Image reference: Map of distant Fátima witness reports]

**Yes—these accounts materially strengthen your response to my crowd-expectation objection.** People elsewhere could not simply have been responding to excitement spreading through the crowd at the Cova.

The strongest records contribute different things:

| Location | Approx. distance | What makes it relevant |
|---|---:|---|
| **Granja** | 157 km | A letter dated **October 14, 1917** reports people seeing solar rotation and a pink cloud. Particularly important because it is next-day documentation, although the writer relays unnamed observers. |
| **Alburitel** | 13 km | The school account describes a pale rotating disc, zigzag descent, fear and colors on surrounding objects. Detailed overlap with the Cova reports, preserved in later testimony. |
| **Minde vicinity** | 13 km | Albano Barros explicitly recalled a falling Sun **“in the direction of Fátima.”** A later interview, with the exact observation location unresolved. |
| **Leiria** | 17 km | Guilhermina Lopes da Silva recalled a great red flash toward the mountain and calling two workmen to see it. |
| **Torres Novas** | 21 km | A November 1917 letter reports something unusual in the Sun at the same hour, explicitly less impressive than at Fátima. |
| **São Pedro de Moel / Oeiras** | 34 / 119 km | Additional geographically separated accounts, preserved through later publications and recollections. |

These distinctions come from our [source-and-location audit](research/fatima-distant-witnesses-20261027/research-report.txt), including the contemporary [Granja letter](https://fatima-1917.com/pt/d/iii-1-79) and [Torres Novas letter](https://fatima-1917.com/pt/d/iii-1-319).

**What this does to my argument:** an adequate ordinary explanation must address geographically dispersed observations, rather than merely explain an excited religious gathering. That is a substantial additional burden.

Two limits still matter:

- **Distance from the crowd does not automatically mean absence of expectation.** The Alburitel hill account explicitly describes advance preparations, including smoked glass.
- **The map does not yet establish converging sightlines to one object above the Cova.** Most accounts lack measured directions and precise observation times. Their geographical spread is established more securely than triangulation.

Neither limitation erases the testimony. My assessment is that **your Fátima argument remains standing against the objection I presented**. The distant accounts strengthen it; I have not supplied an ordinary explanation that adequately accounts for the combined evidence.

messages.text:
Yes. **The argument I’ll try to sustain is that Pio’s fragrance reports are less discriminating between supernatural and ordinary causes than you maintain—even accepting that witnesses genuinely smelled something.**

Here is the argument:

1. **Intermittency does not rule out an ordinary odor.** Muse argues that applied perfume would be perceived continuously. But Pamela Dalton and Charles Wysocki, researchers at the **Monell Chemical Senses Center**, experimentally demonstrated reduced sensitivity during continued odor exposure. A continuing source need not produce a continuing conscious perception. That challenges a specific exclusion of ordinary fragrance; it does not establish what happened around Pio. [Their study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8710455/)

2. **An unsuspecting witness establishes more than suggestion, but not necessarily supernatural origin.** Rome surgeon **Giorgio Festa’s** account of people spontaneously noticing fragrance from the transported bloodstained cloth is substantial evidence of a real scented object. We must examine whether its handling and subsequent behavior distinguish an extraordinary source from an ordinarily scented object. [Account reproduced by Muse](https://motivacredibilitatis.substack.com/p/st-pio-of-pietrelcina)

3. **Remote and post-death reports require an additional attribution step.** Two people independently noticing roses is stronger than one person imagining them. Nevertheless, identifying that smell with Pio requires evidence beyond its pleasantness and religious setting.

**My burden is to show that these distinctions materially weaken the strongest episodes taken together.** Merely saying “perhaps perfume” or correcting one sentence about intermittency would not defeat your core argument.

Conversely, if the strongest records establish repeated fragrance under circumstances that substantially exclude ordinary sources—and securely connect those occurrences to Pio—my proposed objection loses. Historical testimony can establish that; I won’t require a modern laboratory experiment as the only acceptable evidence.

messages.text:
**There are explicit reports of people not detecting the fragrance. I haven’t located a named firsthand account saying Pio himself smelled foul.** Those are different findings.

The clearest non-detections are:

| Person | What the account says |
|---|---|
| **Fr. Pietro**, a Capuchin superior | Did not perceive fragrance in Pio’s room, but did in the vegetable garden. |
| **People accompanying Fr. Lorenzo** | Bishop **Raffaello Carlo Rossi’s** investigation records Lorenzo perceiving fragrance while others with him did not. The quoted passage does not identify those others individually. |
| **Fr. Agostino da San Marco in Lamis**, Pio’s confessor | Reportedly entered his room, spoke with him and handled bloodstained handkerchiefs repeatedly without detecting fragrance—before reporting an experience in September 1931. |
| **Rome surgeon Giorgio Festa** | Personally detected nothing because he lacked a sense of smell. **That makes him unsuitable as a negative witness**, although he recorded other people’s spontaneous reactions. |

These passages are reproduced in [Muse’s fragrance section](https://motivacredibilitatis.substack.com/p/st-pio-of-pietrelcina).

Importantly, **Agostino Gemelli—the Franciscan physician, psychologist and founder of Milan’s Catholic University—did not simply deny an odor existed**. His April 1920 report describes an aromatic smell emanating from Pio’s hands. His 1926 report describes a less intense mixture of odors associated with the room, habit and gloves, disputing its localization and supernatural interpretation. He does **not** describe foul body odor in those passages. [Gemelli’s published reports, PDF pages 5 and 12](https://r2.padrepauloricardo.org/uploads/anexo/arquivo/4676/contro-padre-pio-por-agostino-gemelli_1695773803.pdf)

On your earlier counting question: **Capuchin Alberto D’Apolito claimed “hundreds of thousands” of people had experienced and reported it.** That is a published estimate of people, **not a verified count of written depositions**. The official Padre Pio portal describes very numerous collected testimonies without providing a numerical inventory. [D’Apolito quotation reproduced by Muse](https://motivacredibilitatis.substack.com/p/st-pio-of-pietrelcina), [official portal](https://www.padrepio.it/il-profumo-di-padre-pio/)

So far, the negative testimony supports **intermittent and selective detection**, which your argument already includes. It does not establish that the fragrance tradition was invented or that Pio ordinarily smelled unpleasant.

**You can already make a reasonable inference to metaphysics.** There isn’t a hidden additional requirement that only appears after your evidence survives scrutiny.

The connecting argument is:

> These events are not merely unusual. Their timing, apparent purpose, reported behavior and religious content fit intentional Christian intervention better than the available ordinary explanations.

That is a **positive explanatory argument**, and you have been making it. Fátima’s announced sign, Zeitoun’s reportedly recognizable figure and purposeful gestures, and Pio’s Christ-associated wounds contribute differently to it.

What would move that inference toward **“best explanation”** is a comparison on four questions:

1. **What happened securely enough to require explanation?** Identify the strongest observations without making disputed embellishments essential.
2. **Does the evidence indicate intention?** A fulfilled announcement or responsive, meaningful behavior bears more directly on agency than an unexplained light or smell alone.
3. **Which explanation fits with fewer unsupported additions?** An ordinary explanation needs evidence and a credible fit. Supernatural intervention also needs a reason to identify the agent and purpose.
4. **Does the combination add independent weight?** Different phenomena, witnesses and settings can strengthen the same explanation. We should account for their real connections without treating those connections as automatic disqualifications.

**You do not have to prove every conceivable ordinary explanation impossible.** Nor would explaining one lesser episode ordinarily erase the strongest remaining cases.

If your central evidence survives a serious examination, positively supports purposeful Christian agency, and the competing explanations remain substantially less adequate, then **I should judge Christian intervention the leading explanation**—rather than indefinitely withhold judgment because supernatural causes initially seem unusual.

Forty successful defenses would matter according to what survives: preserving the central evidence of prediction, public manifestation and agency would be much more consequential than winning forty peripheral disputes. The connector you’re asking for is already present in your argument; our remaining work is to assess its comparative strength consistently.

**My strongest documented challenge concerns Fátima: whether the reported colors and rotation establish an extraordinary external light source.**

**Domingos Pinto Coelho**, a Catholic lawyer who attended October 13, described the apparent rotation, changing colors and approach toward Earth. But in *A Ordem* on October 16, he also reported a subsequent comparison: watching the Sun partly covered by clouds, he again experienced—in my translation—“the same succession of colors, the same rotational movement, etc.” This is his contemporary account, rather than a skeptic’s later speculation. [Original report](https://fatima-1917.com/pt/d/iii-1-97).

The argument I would defend is:

1. A participant reported experiencing important features again under apparently ordinary solar-viewing conditions.
2. That supplies positive evidence that those features can arise without an extraordinary object moving overhead.
3. Consequently, thousands reporting those features does not, by itself, distinguish a miraculous external source from many people observing the same Sun and experiencing similar visual effects. Their sincerity remains intact.

**Muse addresses this directly.** He cites Portuguese historian **Costa Brochado’s** criticism that Coelho exaggerated the resemblance, and Maria de Jesus Raposo’s judgment that later solar effects differed substantially from October 13. That is relevant counterevidence. However, another witness distinguishing her experiences does not establish that Coelho inaccurately compared his own. Brochado’s proposed political motivation also needs evidence beyond disagreement with Coelho’s conclusion. [Muse’s response, §5.3](https://motivacredibilitatis.substack.com/p/it-wasnt-the-sun).

There are real limits: Coelho did not conduct a controlled experiment, and his repeat description does **not explicitly establish that he reproduced the full frightening descent**. He also clarified the following day that he was not disputing other people’s different observations or categorically denying a miracle. [His clarification](https://fatima-1917.com/pt/d/iii-1-109).

**The conclusion I’m arguing for is therefore specific:** colors and apparent rotation have a documented ordinary alternative and cannot carry the supernatural inference on their own. The prediction, fuller movement, environmental effects and distant testimony must establish the distinction.

That is a substantive challenge to part of your case. It is not yet an explanation of Fátima as a whole.

**Next: does Pio’s fragrance add strong independent evidence of a miracle to the stigmata?**

I would start with **Dr. Giorgio Festa’s transported cloth**, because it addresses your strongest objection to suggestion: people reportedly noticed the fragrance without knowing he carried it.

Festa describes taking a bloodstained cloth away, passengers noticing its scent, and the cloth subsequently scenting his consulting room. My argument is that **this particular sequence also fits a real odor carried by material**. The report establishes fragrance more directly than it establishes how that fragrance originated. [Festa’s published report, printed pp.205–206](https://www.imagomundi.biz/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/PBSO37-Le_stigmate_di_Padre_Pio_da_Pietrelcina-Gerardo_di_Flumeri.pdf).

Intermittency and differences between observers do not independently exclude that possibility. **Pamela Dalton and Charles Wysocki of Monell Chemical Senses Center** experimentally demonstrated that continuing odor exposure can reduce sensitivity and perceived intensity. [Study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8710455/).

**The proposition I’m defending:** those observations can be sincere without requiring either supernatural scent production or knowing accomplices.

The substantial burden on my argument is the rest of your case: recurrent fragrance over decades, unsuspecting observers, and remote or posthumous experiences. I have not identified an ordinary source that accounts for that entire pattern. This challenge therefore concerns how much the strongest documented scent observations discriminate between the explanations—not whether people smelled something.
